conclusion.label: endorses

report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **supported by moderate-quality evidence, with important nuance**: Anti-cytokine drugs appear to reduce depressive symptoms in people with chronic inflammatory conditions, but the effect is likely driven by improvement in the underlying inflammatory disease and appears strongest in patients who already have elevated inflammation.

The best evidence comes from Kappelmann et al.'s systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical trials in chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis) where depressive symptoms were a secondary outcome. Across roughly 20 trials, anti-cytokine treatments (including TNF-antagonists and other cytokine modulators) showed a moderate, statistically significant antidepressant effect (Cohen's d ≈ 0.4) compared with placebo (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794896/; https://www.nature.com/articles/mp2016167). The authors interpret this as suggesting a potentially causal role for cytokines in depression, though they note effects could partly reflect improvement in physical illness/quality of life rather than a direct antidepressant mechanism.

This is corroborated by a separate randomized trial (Raison et al.) of the TNF-antagonist infliximab in treatment-resistant depression (not solely inflammatory disease patients), which found no overall antidepressant benefit, but did find improvement specifically in the subgroup with elevated baseline inflammatory markers (CRP) (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/1356541).

**Caveats**: Effects are heterogeneous across trials, depression was usually a secondary rather than primary endpoint, and benefits seem inflammation-dependent rather than universal.

**Sources**: PMC5794896, Nature mp2016167, JAMA Psychiatry 1356541.
